The principal issues that arise for our consideration on the basis of the submissions made by the Petitioner and TPCL are as follows: _The Commission may, at any stage of the proceedings in a petition, allow either party to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy between the parties:_ _The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties:_ pleadings. The first requirement relates to the necessity of the amendment to determine the real controversy between the parties. The expression “real controversy” refers to the dispute which forms the subject matter of the proceedings as originally instituted. Amendments are ordinarily permitted where they clarify existing pleadings, bring on record subsequent developments closely connected with the original cause of action, or assist the adjudicatory body in effectively determining the issues already arising in the proceedings. However, amendments which introduce an entirely new set of claims or shift the focus of the proceedings to issues that were not part of the original lis cannot be regarded as necessary to determine the real controversy. Applying the above principles to the present case, we note that the original Petition was primarily instituted to seek enforcement of the directions issued by the MoP dated 20.2.2023 under Section 11(1) of the Act, and initiation of proceedings under Sections 142 and 146 of the Act for alleged non-compliance with such statutory directions. The reliefs sought were therefore essentially prospective and regulatory in nature, namely directions requiring TPCL to generate and supply electricity in accordance with the Section 11 directions and to declare availability against the contracted capacity. introducing monetary claims and contractual issues which were not part of the original lis. Even in the absence of demonstrable prejudice, such a fundamental shift in the nature of the proceedings cannot be permitted within the framework of the present Petition. The Petition, as originally framed, seeks enforcement of statutory directions and initiation of proceedings for alleged non-compliance under Sections 142 and 146 of the Act. Proceedings under Sections 142 and 146 are regulatory and quasi-penal in character and are concerned with determining whether a statutory direction has been contravened and whether penal consequences should follow. The amendment now sought seeks to introduce extensive monetary claims and contractual issues arising under the PPA, thereby converting the proceedings from one primarily concerned with statutory compliance and penal consequences into a proceeding seeking adjudication of monetary restitution. The cause of action in the original Petition was singular and self-contained, namely, alleged non-compliance with statutory directions issued under Section 11(1). In contrast, the cause of action now sought to be introduced pertains to non-supply of power and resultant financial loss under the PPA, which falls within an entirely different legal domain.
